TimeFocus.q: You are leading a project meeting with an international team. The agenda has 5 items, but the first topic sparks a rich, unexpected discussion. The scheduled time has passed. What do you do?
options: Politely interrupt and move to the next agenda item. The schedule must be respected.
Allow 2-3 extra minutes, then firmly redirect the group back to the agenda.
Quickly assess whether the discussion is more valuable than remaining items and adjust accordingly.
Let the discussion continue and drop the least important agenda item to compensate.
Fully embrace the organic flow. The best outcomes come from following the energy of the group.

TimeFocus.q: A colleague calls during your focused work time for a non-urgent matter. How do you respond?
options: I don't answer. I have blocked this time for deep work and will call back during open hours.
I answer briefly, explain I'm busy, and schedule a specific time to talk later.
I answer and spend a few minutes helping, then gently wrap up.
I take the call and help as long as needed. Relationships come first.
I'm happy to help. Interruptions are a natural part of the workday.

TimeFocus.q: You are organizing a social event for an international group. How do you structure the evening?
options: A detailed timeline: 7:00 arrivals, 7:30 dinner, 8:30 speeches, 9:30 networking, 10:30 close.
A loose framework with approximate start times but some flexibility built in.
A general plan (dinner, then socializing) but I let the evening unfold naturally.
Minimal structure. I provide food, drinks, and a space, and trust the group.
No schedule at all. People arrive when they arrive, eat when hungry, leave when ready.

TimeOrientation.q: Your organization is considering a major strategic change. What type of argument do you find most persuasive?
options: This approach has been tested for decades and has a proven track record.
This builds on established traditions while making careful, incremental improvements.
This respects our history but also positions us for emerging trends.
This is innovative and will give us a competitive advantage in the next 5 years.
This completely reimagines our model. We need to disrupt ourselves before someone else does.

TimeOrientation.q: A diplomatic delegation is visiting your city. What do you prioritize in the welcome program?
options: Historical monuments, museums, and sites showcasing our rich heritage.
A mix of historical sites and meetings with established institutions.
A balanced program honoring past achievements while showcasing current developments.
Tours of innovation hubs, tech parks, and startups showing where our country is heading.
Presentations on future megaprojects and emerging industries that don't exist yet.

TimeOrientation.q: When making an important personal decision (e.g., relocating), what weighs most heavily?
options: How this honors my family's history, roots, and previous generations' sacrifices.
Whether this is consistent with values and lessons from my past experiences.
A balance between honoring where I come from and creating new opportunities.
How this positions me for growth and success in the coming years.
The long-term vision of the life I want to build 10-20 years from now.

Space.q: You are working in a shared office with international colleagues. How do you feel about the workspace?
options: I need a closed door and clear boundaries. My workspace is my personal territory.
I prefer a quiet corner or partitioned desk with some visual and acoustic privacy.
I'm comfortable in open-plan if private meeting rooms are available when needed.
I enjoy open, shared spaces where I can interact with colleagues throughout the day.
I thrive in bustling, communal environments. The more people around, the more energized.

Space.q: A new colleague asks a personal question (salary, marital status) during work lunch. How do you react?
options: Very uncomfortable. This is private and has no place in a professional setting.
I give a vague, polite answer and steer back to work topics.
I share a little to be friendly but keep most details to myself.
I'm open to sharing. Knowing each other personally builds stronger professional trust.
I welcome it enthusiastically. There is no separation between personal and professional life.

Space.q: When hosting an international business dinner, how do you handle seating?
options: Assigned seats with clear place cards. Each person has their designated space.
Assigned seats for key guests, some flexibility for others.
General seating plan (this table for delegation, that for our team) but no specific seats.
Open seating. I encourage people to mix and sit wherever comfortable.
No seating plan. Everyone shares food family-style and moves around freely.

Power.q: During a negotiation, the most senior person on your team makes a statement with a factual error. What do you do?
options: I correct the error immediately and openly. Accuracy matters more than rank.
I raise my hand: 'If I may add a clarification...' in a respectful but direct tone.
I wait for a natural pause and gently reframe without explicitly calling it an error.
I say nothing during the meeting but send a private message afterward.
I would never contradict a senior leader in front of others. Their authority must be preserved.

Power.q: You are at a formal diplomatic reception. How do you approach greeting protocol?
options: I greet everyone equally with a handshake and first names, regardless of title.
I use titles for the most senior but am more casual with junior staff.
I follow my host's lead. If formal, I match; if casual, I match.
I research the hierarchy beforehand and greet the most senior person first with formalities.
I strictly observe all protocol: bowing, waiting to be introduced, full titles, deferring throughout.

Power.q: In a cross-cultural team project, how should decisions be made?
options: Every member has an equal vote regardless of position. The best idea wins.
Everyone shares opinions, but the team lead makes the final call.
The team discusses openly; the most experienced members naturally guide toward consensus.
The senior leader consults a small inner circle, then announces the decision.
The most senior person decides. Their authority makes them best suited to lead.

Structure.q: Your company offers you a prestigious individual award, but your team contributed significantly. How do you handle it?
options: I accept proudly. I earned it through individual effort and initiative.
I accept but publicly acknowledge my team's contributions in my speech.
I feel uncomfortable accepting alone and suggest sharing with the team.
I redirect recognition to the team. Group success matters more than individual achievement.
I decline the individual award and insist it go to the entire team.

Structure.q: You are assigned to a long-term project abroad. What is your primary relationship-building goal?
options: To expand my personal professional network and advance my individual career.
To build a few strong professional connections for mutual future benefit.
To integrate into the local community while maintaining independence and personal goals.
To become a trusted group member, prioritizing their needs alongside my own.
To fully immerse in the group's identity. My success is inseparable from the community's.

Structure.q: When facing a major life decision, whose opinion matters most?
options: My own. I trust my individual judgment above all else.
My own, but I value input from a close friend or mentor.
A balance between personal desires and family/close circle expectations.
My family and close community. Their well-being and approval are central.
The collective. I would not decide without full consensus from family and community.

Competition.q: In a business pitch competition, another team struggles with their technology. What do you do?
options: I focus on my own preparation. We are competitors; it's not my responsibility.
I wish them luck but don't intervene. Fair competition means managing your own challenges.
I offer a quick suggestion if I know the solution, but don't go out of my way.
I actively help them fix the issue. A good relationship matters more than winning.
I share my equipment freely. The best outcome is when everyone presents their best work.

Competition.q: Your company is setting performance targets. What approach do you advocate?
options: Individual targets with clear rankings and bonuses for top performers.
Individual targets with some team-based incentives to balance drive with collaboration.
A mix of individual and team goals with equal weight.
Team-based targets where the group succeeds or fails together.
Collective organizational goals only. Internal competition is destructive.

Competition.q: In a cross-cultural workshop, which group exercise format do you prefer?
options: A competitive debate where teams argue opposing positions and a winner is declared.
Structured exercise with scoring, but teams can learn from each other.
Collaborative problem-solving where all groups work on the same challenge and share results.
A cooperative simulation where all participants work together for a single shared outcome.
A community-building circle focused on mutual understanding, not producing a result.

Communication.q: You receive an email: 'Your proposal is interesting. We will think about it and get back to you when the time is right.' How do you interpret this?
options: They are genuinely interested and will contact me soon with specific feedback.
They are leaning positive but need more time. I'll follow up in a week.
I'm not sure. The message is ambiguous, so I'll wait and ask for clarification.
This is likely a polite refusal. 'Interesting' and 'when the time is right' suggest they won't say no directly.
This is clearly a 'no.' Direct rejection would be rude, so they signal refusal indirectly.

Communication.q: You need to give negative feedback to a colleague about their presentation. How do you deliver it?
options: Directly: 'Your presentation had three major issues. Here they are...'
Honestly but constructively: 'Good effort, but specific areas need improvement.'
Carefully, balancing positive and negative so the message is clear but not harsh.
Indirectly, by asking questions that guide them to identify issues themselves.
Very subtly, through hints or a trusted third party. Direct criticism would damage the relationship.

Communication.q: Your counterpart says 'yes' but their body language is hesitant. How do you proceed?
options: I take the 'yes' at face value and move forward with the agreement.
I note the hesitation but proceed, planning to confirm details in writing later.
I pause and ask: 'Are you comfortable with all aspects of this proposal?'
I read the non-verbal cues as discomfort and suggest revisiting with more flexibility.
The 'yes' is about harmony, not agreement. I slow down, rebuild rapport, and look for the real answer in what is NOT said.

Action.q: You meet a new international contact at a conference. What do you want to know first?
options: What do they do? Job title, company, current projects.
Their professional achievements and goals they're working toward.
A mix of what they do professionally and who they are as a person.
Where they're from, their family, what they enjoy outside work.
Who they are at their core—values, philosophy, what gives them meaning.

Action.q: Your organization evaluates a partnership's success. What metric matters most?
options: Tangible results: revenue, contracts signed, deadlines met.
Measurable outcomes combined with qualitative stakeholder feedback.
A balance between deliverables and relationship quality built during the process.
The depth of trust and mutual understanding established between partners.
The long-term harmony and shared purpose that emerged, regardless of short-term deliverables.

Action.q: When introducing yourself to international professionals, how do you describe yourself?
options: I'm a [title] at [company]. I specialize in [field] and recently completed [achievement].
I work in [field] and I'm passionate about [goal]. Currently focused on [project].
I work in [field], but I'm also a [hobby/identity]. I believe in balancing professional and personal growth.
I value deep connections and meaningful experiences. My relationships define me more than my title.
I'm a [cultural identity] who believes in [philosophy]. My work is just one expression of who I am.
